title: Diamond optomechanical crystals for high-frequency strain and comb generation
authors: Elham Zohari, Waleed El-Sayed, Aria Jafari, Ahmas El-hamamsy, Peyman Parsa, Joseph E. Losby, Natália C. Carvalho, Paul E. Barclay
abstract: Quantum optomechanical technologies benefit from mechanical oscillators that are high-frequency, can be coherently driven, and are capable of coupling to other quantum systems. Diamond supports all of these criteria: its large elastic modulus increases mechanical resonance frequency, its low nonlinear optical absorption increases the allowed intensity of fields used for coherent optomechanics, and it hosts spin qubits that interact with mechanical modes. Here we demonstrate a diamond optomechanical crystal cavity that supports multiple mechanical resonances with $\sim$12 GHz frequency and high $Q_\text{m} \times f_\text{m}$ product that can be coherently coupled to multiple optical modes. By exciting this sideband resolved system into mechanical self-sustained oscillations, we generate a frequency comb spanning 143 GHz. Analysis of the comb spectrum, combined with systematic characterization of the system's optomechanical coupling, allows us to quantitatively show that its mechanical oscillation amplitude reaches 130 pm. This corresponds to a maximum total dynamic strain of $1.1 \times 10^{-3}$ that is sufficiently high for future demonstrations of optomechanical control of diamond spin qubits.
summary: Researchers developed a diamond optomechanical crystal cavity to enhance quantum optomechanical coupling. By achieving self-sustained mechanical oscillations, the device generates a large-scale optical frequency comb. This demonstrates a high dynamic strain, making the platform highly promising for controlling diamond spin qubits using light.
main_problem: The goal is to demonstrate a diamond optomechanical crystal cavity capable of generating a high-frequency optical frequency comb while achieving a large dynamic strain for future quantum control applications.
main_result: The system successfully generates an optical frequency comb spanning 143 GHz, corresponding to a maximum dynamic strain of $1.1 	imes 10^{-3}$ in the mechanical oscillation.
method: The study combines theoretical simulation (COMSOL) for device design and characterization with experimental measurements of cavity resonances and frequency comb generation under self-sustained oscillation.
model_or_system: The platform is a diamond optomechanical crystal (OMC) cavity, which leverages diamond's high elastic modulus, low absorption, and inherent spin qubits. The system supports multiple optical and mechanical resonances that are coupled via the optomechanical interaction.
key_observables: Frequency comb spectrum (143 GHz span), peak mechanical oscillation amplitude (130 pm), total dynamic strain ($1.1 	imes 10^{-3}$), and optomechanical coupling rate ($g_0$).
important_parameters: Mechanical resonance frequency ($\sim 12$ GHz), high mechanical quality factor ($Q_m 	imes f_m$), and the resolved-sideband regime ($\omega_m > \kappa_{tot}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the system operates in the resolved-sideband regime and requires careful modeling to account for photothermal shifts when determining the effective detuning.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the OMC cavity schematic, mode profiles (optical and mechanical), transmission spectra showing resonances, and the final frequency comb structure via sideband analysis.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from device design and mode characterization (simulations) to demonstrating the transition from thermal motion to self-sustained oscillation, culminating in the quantitative measurement and analysis of the generated frequency comb.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the coupling of mechanical motion to optical fields in a solid-state quantum system (diamond), which is a cornerstone of cavity QED and optomechanics for quantum information processing.
